profile.reading:
Switch Las Vegas 14 sits at 5680 Badura Avenue, Las Vegas, Nevada, on Switch's Core Campus in unincorporated Clark County; this record's own OpenStreetMap tags include an explicit "ref=14" and "operator=Switch," giving strong confidence in both the building's identity and its Switch ownership even without a dedicated Switch spec page. Switch's own current site does not publish individual square footage, megawatt capacity, year-opened, or redundancy-design figures for Las Vegas 14; the only material available for this building is its own confirmed address plus Switch's general Core Campus marketing, which states up to 495 megawatts of power upon completion and 100 percent renewable energy across the full campus. Switch has separately announced two new, smaller "AI Factory" buildings on nearby Jones Boulevard and Roy Horn Way in July 2025, roughly 199,000 and 228,000 square feet respectively, denser and more specialized than the older numbered colocation buildings like Las Vegas 14, illustrating how Switch's Las Vegas campus has begun shifting toward AI-specific infrastructure alongside its legacy enterprise colocation buildings. Switch's Nevada tax-advantages materials describe a consumer-use-tax abatement to as low as 2 percent and a 75 percent property-tax abatement on customer equipment at Switch facilities, administered through Nevada's Governor's Office of Economic Development. Switch does not name a specific power utility on its Las Vegas pages, though NV Energy is the incumbent utility across Clark County as a matter of public record.

Clark County's data center cluster, anchored substantially by Switch's Core Campus, has helped establish Las Vegas as a significant secondary U.S. data center market outside the major coastal and Northern Virginia hubs, drawing additional colocation and hyperscale investment from other operators over the past decade. Switch's original 2002 founding purchase, a former Enron-affiliated facility acquired at auction for 930,000 dollars, sat over a fiber-optic backbone corridor that shaped the campus's subsequent growth pattern along South Decatur Boulevard, West Capovilla Avenue, Lindell Road, and Badura Avenue, the streets along which most of Switch's Core Campus buildings, including this one, are addressed.

reading.body:
Switch Las Vegas 14 is a numbered colocation building on Switch's Core Campus in unincorporated Clark County, Nevada, one of eleven operating facilities across the campus that Switch does not individually specify in published capacity or design figures. The Core Campus as a whole is designed to reach 495 megawatts upon completion and will use 100 percent renewable energy, though the operator publishes no breakdown by building. Las Vegas 14 sits on Badura Avenue in the fiber corridor that has anchored Switch's campus growth since the company acquired a former Enron facility in 2002, positioning it within the same infrastructure footprint as the campus's larger developments.

Switch is simultaneously building denser, AI-specialized facilities on the same Las Vegas campus, with two new AI Factories announced for 2025 totaling roughly 427,000 square feet on Jones Boulevard and Roy Horn Way, separate from legacy numbered colocation buildings like this one. This shift suggests Las Vegas 14 functions as part of Switch's enterprise colocation and cloud services footprint rather than as a dedicated AI training platform, though the operator does not publish tenant names or workload types for any building on the campus.

Nevada publishes no megawatt figures for Las Vegas 14 in available operator specifications, leaving the building's actual capacity and utilization unmeasured in this registry. Switch Las Vegas 14 ranks third among Nevada facilities with published capacity, though only two facilities in the state publish megawatt figures at all, totaling 10.37 MW across all of Nevada's 26 mapped data centers. This facility's relevance to AI scaling depends entirely on its fraction of the Core Campus's 495 MW endpoint, a figure the operator has chosen not to allocate to individual buildings.
